Speech: “The Weight of Pragmatism—Defending an Imperfect Order in a Dangerous World”

Mr. Chairman, distinguished colleagues,

We gather at a moment when American power, American values, and American security are no longer moving in neat formation. They tug at one another—sometimes violently. And we are obliged, as elected stewards of the republic, to choose between the America we wish existed and the America that must survive.

Idealists tell us that every alliance must be judged by the spotless mirror of democracy and human rights. I come before you today not to deny that mirror, but to ask what happens when it shatters in our hand while our adversaries level theirs at our throat.

Let us be clear-eyed: history rewards survival. And history is littered with democracies that failed because they allowed moral vanity to masquerade as grand strategy. Athens was lost to Sparta when it forgot that alliances of convenience—the Persian navy, Sicilian tyrants—were the only lifeboats in a storm. Britain tolerated a genocidal Russian czar long enough to defeat Napoleon, and FDR toasted a Georgian despot whose labor camps stretched to the Arctic in order to crush Hitlerism.

These were not proud moments. They were embers of wisdom in the furnace of necessity.

America today faces the same grim arithmetic:

  • China has weaponized every sinew of interconnectedness—rare-earth mines in Burma, ports in Djibouti, surveillance batteries in Shenzhen.
  • Russia wages war by buffet: cyber-plunder, energy blackmail, and expeditionary brigades greased by Wagner contracts from Mali to the Central African Republic.
  • Iran’s clerics fund militias in four countries while perfecting centrifuges that bring atomic doom weeks—not years—away.

In such a landscape, the idle luxury of picking only democratic dance partners would end with America dancing alone—until the music stopped forever.

We must therefore ask a harder question than “Does our ally share every one of our values?” The decisive question is: “If we abandon this imperfect partner, do we cede critical ground to an enemy bent on eroding every remaining space where freedom might still breathe tomorrow?”

This is not abandonment of principle; it is stewardship of what remains.

I hate what the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia does to its dissidents. I hate what Egypt’s prisons do to journalists. But I hate even more the prospect of Tehran’s Revolutionary Guards docking frigates in Jeddah, or Beijing embedding Huawei fiber in the Suez, extinguishing what is left of the West’s energy lifelines to Europe and Africa.

This is the cruel mathematics deterrence demands. When nuclear armed rivals probe for flanks, we must fortify lines—even if those lines are guarded by flawed sentries.

Some will say this makes us “no better than they.” The objection is emotionally satisfying and strategically infantile. A surgeon who refuses to cut contaminated flesh because it feels wrong will see the patient die. Likewise, a power that refuses to sully its pristine conscience will soon lecture only ashes.

Our ethical task is compartmentalization, not capitulation:

  • Impose red lines in every alliance—no American weapon shall ever be used to suppress a peaceful majority pleading for votes instead of violence.
  • Leverage our partnership as leverage for calibrated reform—quiet channels, phased arms deliveries, and rigorous benchmarking. The record shows that nations reliant on U.S. logistics and training cannot forever insulate themselves from our norms.
  • Accelerate alliances of first resort among fellow democracies—AUKUS, the Quad, renewed NATO investment—so that ties with autocracies remain what they must be: temporary buffers, not permanent bargains.

And let us speak plainly to the American people: The Constitution you cherish was born not amid purity, but amid compromise with slaveholders. The Emancipation you celebrate was won in an alliance with half a continent that still denied women the vote. The post-war order you revere was cemented by deals with dictators who agreed to stand against a greater tyranny. Perfection has never sailed aboard the ship of state; it walks, limping, behind, begging us to drag it forward.

So I do not stand before you to celebrate dictators. I stand to say that when fire leaps the ridge, one can fight it with imperfect locals who know the terrain or one can watch the blaze consume the entire forest. The choice—amputation today, or autopsy tomorrow—is not one any generation wishes to make. But choose honestly we must.

May God give us the wisdom to wield this armor of necessity without letting it weld to our skin, and the humility to remember that every alliance with a tyrant is a down-payment on a future reckoning we owe to liberty itself.

The Imperative of Realpolitik: Why the United States Must Support Authoritarian Regimes When National Interests Demand It

American foreign policy has long suffered from a destructive tension between professed ideals and actual power realities. The United States should abandon the fiction that it can or should export democracy and human rights as primary objectives. When authoritarian regimes deliver regional stability, secure critical resource flows, or check hostile competitors, Washington must openly support them without apology. Hesitation on moral grounds has repeatedly cost America strategic ground, created power vacuums filled by worse actors, and weakened its own position in an unforgiving international system.

History demonstrates the practical dividend of this approach. During the Cold War, the United States cultivated partnerships with a range of non-democratic governments to contain Soviet expansion. Support for leaders in Turkey, South Korea in its early decades, and Indonesia under Suharto helped anchor anti-communist alliances that ultimately contributed to the Soviet collapse. These relationships were not endorsements of internal governance models; they were instruments for advancing American security and prosperity. Similar logic applied to Gulf monarchies, whose alignment secured energy access and later enabled counterterrorism cooperation against groups that liberal regimes often proved too fragile or ideologically confused to confront effectively. In each case, the alternative—insistence on democratic reforms at the expense of strategic utility—produced instability or invited rival influence.

Stability itself carries independent value. Many regions feature deep ethnic, sectarian, or tribal fractures where rapid democratization has triggered chaos rather than enlightenment. Libya after 2011 illustrates the pattern: removal of a strongman in the name of human rights produced militia rule, migrant flows that destabilized Europe, and opportunities for Russian and Chinese inroads. Egypt's brief experimentation with elected Islamist government before the 2013 return to authoritarian structures showed how ballot-box outcomes can empower forces hostile to American interests. Strong, centralized regimes that maintain borders, police territory, and suppress irredentist movements often outperform the fragile democracies that follow idealistic interventions. The United States benefits when such regimes prevent the emergence of failed states that export terrorism, host insurgencies, or disrupt trade routes.

Resource security reinforces the case. The global economy runs on oil, natural gas, rare earth minerals, and other inputs whose reliable supply depends on territory controlled by governments with limited respect for individual rights. Saudi Arabia remains essential for energy market stability despite its internal practices; withdrawing support or conditioning it on rapid democratization would simply hand pricing influence to actors less aligned with American goals. In Africa and Latin America, China and Russia have demonstrated the alternative model—unconditional engagement with resource-rich authoritarian governments that asks no questions about governance. An American policy that insists on democratic preconditions forfeits market share, strategic footholds, and leverage over adversaries who face fewer domestic constraints. Competition requires matching realism, not unilateral disarmament through moral posturing.

The broader philosophical error lies in treating the nation-state as a dispenser of universal morality rather than a vehicle for its citizens' security and welfare. Governments exist first to protect their own populations, not to reform distant societies. Imposing democratic forms on unwilling or unprepared populations has produced repeated disappointments, from Southeast Asia to the Middle East and Central Asia. Meanwhile, authoritarian transitions to more open systems—South Korea and Taiwan being standard examples—typically occurred after decades of security-induced economic growth, not through external pressure while instability reigned. Pressuring regimes on internal matters often erodes the very leverage needed for cooperation on shared interests such as counter-proliferation or supply-chain resilience.

Critics rightly note that long-term American credibility sometimes suffers from visible alliances with unattractive partners. Yet this objection underestimates the corrosive effect of selective outrage and inconsistent application. Every major power—China with its investments in Africa and Central Asia, Russia with its energy clients, regional actors in the Middle East—pursues interests without democratic litmus tests. Pretending otherwise places America at a competitive disadvantage while achieving little measurable improvement in global human rights. The honest recognition that alliances are transactional tools rather than moral endorsements would actually reduce hypocrisy and allow clearer prioritization of threats.

In practice, this means conditioning support on measurable deliverables: border control, suppression of designated terrorist infrastructure, access to markets or basing rights, and alignment against peer competitors. It does not require public endorsement of every domestic policy, nor does it preclude quiet encouragement of incremental reforms where leverage exists. It simply places strategic outcomes—preventing hostile hegemony, maintaining energy flows, preserving military access—above procedural template conformity. Countries that deliver these outcomes earn partnership regardless of their internal arrangements; those that do not face calibrated pressure regardless of rhetoric.

The alternative of prioritizing human rights and democratic form over interests has already exacted measurable costs in influence, treasure, and strategic position. A policy that openly privileges the latter when they conflict with the former would align American actions with observable reality rather than aspirational theory. In international politics, power ultimately rests on results, not intentions. Regimes that produce favorable results for American security deserve support; those that do not, regardless of their internal righteousness, deserve pragmatic indifference.

Realist foundations of the approach

Realist theorists from Hans Morgenthau onward have argued that states operate in an anarchic system where survival depends on power balances rather than moral consistency. Supporting strong central authorities abroad aligns with this by treating regimes according to their utility in containing rivals like Soviet communism during the Cold War or more recent competitors such as Russia and China.

  • Authoritarian leaders often deliver predictable cooperation on military basing, intelligence sharing, and force projection without the interruptions of domestic elections or opposition parties.

Stability versus transition risks

Proponents claim that abrupt democratization frequently produces volatility worse than controlled authoritarianism. Regimes with strong executive control maintain internal order and border security, limiting spillover effects like refugee flows, weapons proliferation, or terrorism sanctuaries.

  • Examples include long-standing partnerships with Gulf monarchies that stabilized oil production amid regional upheavals, contrasting with the instability following the 2011 Arab Spring in Egypt and Libya.
  • Rapid regime change can empower ideological extremes, as occurred when undermining the Shah in Iran led to a theocratic government more antagonistic to Western interests.
  • Authoritarian continuity allows gradual economic development in select cases, such as South Korea and Taiwan's earlier phases under martial rule that preceded later liberalizations once security was assured.

Resource and economic access

Authoritarian partners frequently offer reliable extraction and trade terms on energy, minerals, and transit routes critical to industrial economies. Transactions proceed without democratic legislatures imposing sanctions or conditionality that raise prices or create supply disruptions.

  • Saudi Arabia and similar states have maintained steady petroleum output and pricing leverage, supporting global markets and funding allied defense capabilities.
  • Deals on rare earths, ports, and pipelines with centralized governments reduce dependency on ideologically aligned but unreliable suppliers.
  • Such arrangements generate commercial advantages for American firms through direct contracts rather than multilateral institutions requiring rights benchmarks.

Geopolitical containment

Securing bases, overflight rights, and joint operations against common threats becomes simpler with decisive leaderships unburdened by parliamentary vetoes or public anti-foreign sentiment. Historical records show these ties contained expansionist powers across continents.

  • Cold War pacts with regimes in Latin America, Southeast Asia, and the Middle East blocked Soviet and Chinese proxy gains without requiring full occupation forces.
  • Modern extensions include counterterrorism cooperation and blocking adversarial footholds in key straits or resource zones.
  • Flexibility in partner selection allows rapid adjustments as threats evolve, unlike fixed commitments to emerging democracies that may align elsewhere.

Limits of democracy-first strategies

Data from decades of interventions indicate mixed or negative returns when resources flow primarily into electoral processes or institutions without underlying order. Successful liberal shifts, such as post-World War II Western Europe, typically followed prior authoritarian consolidation and external threats that aligned incentives.

  • Resources spent conditioning aid on rights improvements often fail against entrenched elites or cultural factors, producing dependency rather than self-sustaining systems.
  • Adversaries exploit the narrative of Western meddling to stoke nationalism, hardening opposition to United States positions.

This perspective treats foreign policy as an instrument for domestic advantage rather than an export of domestic values, accepting trade-offs where ideals conflict with measurable power metrics. Practical application varies by administration, with selectivity applied where transitions align with existing strengths.

In practice, American moral authority is determined by its domestic practices and its treatment of vulnerable populations at home far more than by its foreign policy choices abroad. Countries that dislike American policies will find reasons to criticize regardless of whom America allies with; countries that respect American power will accept cooperation with imperfect partners as a fact of international life.

The Realist Case for Prioritizing Strategic Interests Over Democracy Promotion

Understanding the Theoretical Foundation

The argument for prioritizing stability and resources over democracy promotion in foreign policy rests primarily on the theory of political realism. This perspective, with roots in the work of thinkers like Hans Morgenthau, Kenneth Waltz, and Henry Kissinger, posits that the international system is inherently anarchic—no central authority exists to protect states, so each must rely on its own power to ensure survival. From this vantage point, morality and ideology are secondary concerns; what matters is maintaining a favorable balance of power and protecting core national interests.

Realists argue that the international system is fundamentally different from domestic politics, where enforceable laws and institutions create conditions for cooperation. In the anarchic realm of international relations, states cannot afford to be idealistic. They must act strategically, forming alliances with whoever can help them maintain power and pursuing interests wherever they find them—whether those partners are democracies or authoritarian regimes.

Core Arguments Supporting This Approach

Stability Over Ideological Purity

Proponents of this policy orientation emphasize that political stability serves broader American interests more reliably than ideological alignment. Democratic transitions are inherently turbulent processes. Societies undergoing democratization often experience political fragmentation, economic disruption, and sometimes violent conflict—all of which can produce outcomes harmful to US interests. A authoritarian government that maintains order, honors its international commitments, and provides a predictable environment for commerce may be more valuable to American strategic goals than a democracy mired in internal crisis.

The argument extends to regional stability. Authoritarian regimes often possess the coercive capacity to prevent state failure, contain extremism, and manage conflicts in ways that fledgling democracies cannot. When such regimes serve as bulwarks against chaos, terrorism, or rival powers, their domestic governance becomes a secondary concern. The Soviet Union's role in defeating Nazi Germany, despite its totalitarian nature, exemplifies how strategic necessity can override ideological opposition.

Resource Access and Economic Interests

A frank realist analysis acknowledges that access to natural resources—oil, minerals, strategic materials—sustains modern economies and military capabilities. Many resource-rich regions are governed by authoritarian regimes precisely because centralized control facilitates resource extraction. Countries like Saudi Arabia, Kazakhstan, or Equatorial Guinea may rank poorly on democratic indices, yet they provide reliable access to commodities essential to American industry and defense.

Supporters argue this isn't merely about greed—it's about economic interdependence creating conditions for eventual liberalization. Engaging with authoritarian regimes brings their elites into contact with Western businesses, creates economic stakes in stable international order, and may over time generate pressures for reform from within. This "strategic engagement" approach envisions economic integration as a slow engine of change, even if immediate political transformation doesn't occur.

Countering Rival Powers

A particularly consequential argument involves great power competition. When authoritarian states serve as strategic partners against peer or near-peer competitors, their internal governance becomes a cost of doing business. The Allied powers' alliance with Stalin's Soviet Union against Nazi Germany, or America's support for anti-communist authoritarian regimes during the Cold War, illustrate this logic: the enemy of my enemy is my friend, regardless of that friend's domestic practices.

In contemporary terms, this argument suggests that pressuring or abandoning authoritarian partners simply because they don't meet Western democratic standards plays into the hands of rival powers—China, Russia, or Iran—who would happily fill the vacuum. The choice isn't between authoritarianism and democracy; it's between having influence with an imperfect partner or ceding influence entirely to competitors.

Pragmatic Limitations of Democracy Promotion

Critics of aggressive democracy promotion point to its mixed historical record. The Iraq War's aftermath demonstrated that military intervention to install democratic governance can produce catastrophic instability, civilian suffering, and outcomes worse than the prior authoritarian order. Even when democracy promotion succeeds electorally, it frequently produces governments hostile to American interests, as Egyptian voters chose the Muslim Brotherhood after Hosni Mubarak's fall.

From this perspective, the United States should learn from experience about the limits of its ability to shape other societies' political development. American officials consistently underestimate local conditions, overestimate their capacity to engineer outcomes, and fail to anticipate how their interventions will be received by populations with different histories and values. A more modest approach accepts that other nations' political systems are ultimately their own concern, focusing American efforts on areas where genuine influence exists.

Historical Precedents

Cold War strategy provides the most extensive laboratory for examining this approach. The United States supported authoritarian regimes across Latin America, Asia, and Africa not despite their undemocratic nature but precisely because anti-communist credentials mattered more than democratic governance. Chile under Pinochet, Mobutu's Zaire, South Korea before democratization, and numerous other cases reflected judgment that imperfect partners were preferable to communist alternatives.

This approach's proponents note that many of these same countries eventually democratized, suggesting that stability and development may be preconditions for democracy rather than democracy being a precondition for stability. South Korea's economic growth under authoritarian rule created the middle class that eventually demanded political voice. The argument isn't that authoritarianism is desirable, but that it may be a stage in development that cannot be bypassed through external pressure.

The Case Against This Approach

This realist framework faces substantial criticism on multiple grounds. First, empirical evidence questions whether stable authoritarianism reliably produces democracy. China has experienced decades of economic growth without political liberalization, suggesting the transition from authoritarianism to democracy is neither automatic nor inevitable. Many authoritarian regimes prove quite durable, meaning "stability" may mean indefinite postponement of democratic governance.

Second, moral arguments insist that strategic interests cannot entirely override human rights concerns. When America backs brutal regimes—providing diplomatic cover, economic support, and sometimes military assistance—it becomes complicit in repression. This compromises American credibility when criticizing other human rights violators and may generate long-term backlash as populations remember who supported their oppressors.

Third, strategic feedback effects complicate the calculus. Supporting authoritarianism may produce short-term stability while creating long-term instability. Repressed populations eventually rebel, producing the very disruptions that intervention was meant to prevent. The Arab Spring demonstrated how seemingly stable authoritarian systems could collapse rapidly when external support structures weakened or when triggered by external shocks.

Fourth, alliance quality arguments suggest that democratic allies tend to be more reliable partners. Research indicates that democracies are less likely to cheat on agreements, more predictable in their behavior, and produce better long-term alignment than authoritarian partners whose interests may shift with leadership changes. The apparent strategic convenience of authoritarian allies may be illusory.

The argument for prioritizing strategic interests over democracy promotion rests on defensible theoretical foundations and historical precedents. It correctly identifies the limits of American capacity to reshape other societies, acknowledges that unstable democracies can be worse than stable authoritarians, and recognizes the importance of great power competition. However, it understates the moral costs of complicity in repression, the strategic risks of depending on unreliable authoritarian partners, and the possibility that a world of stable authoritarianism may not serve American interests as well as one of expanding democracy.

Most contemporary foreign policy practitioners adopt middle positions—seeking to balance strategic engagement with selective pressure on human rights, avoiding both naive idealism and cynical Realpolitik. The debate remains vigorous precisely because neither pure realism nor pure idealism offers adequate guidance through the complexities of international relations.

The Case for Realism: Why America Should Embrace Its Authoritarian Partners

Introduction

For decades, American foreign policy has been torn between two impulses: the pragmatic pursuit of national interest and the aspirational promotion of democracy and human rights. This tension has produced the worst of both worlds—a policy of selective moralism that convinces no one, constrains American action, and repeatedly leads the United States into catastrophic interventions. It is time for the United States to abandon the pretense and embrace an openly realist foreign policy: one that supports authoritarian regimes and dictators without apology whenever doing so serves American strategic interests, whether in ensuring regional stability, securing critical resources, or countering great-power rivals. The internal governance of other nations is not America's responsibility. The security and prosperity of American citizens is.

The First Duty of Government Is to Its Own Citizens

The fundamental premise of moralistic foreign policy—that the United States bears responsibility for how foreign governments treat their own people—is philosophically confused. The American government derives its legitimacy from the American people, and its obligations run to them alone. A president who sacrifices tangible American interests—energy security, counterterrorism cooperation, strategic positioning—in order to punish a foreign regime for its domestic conduct has betrayed his constituents in favor of people who did not elect him and cannot hold him accountable.

This is not callousness; it is the basic logic of statehood. In an anarchic international system, no higher authority exists to enforce order or protect American interests. Nations that subordinate their interests to abstract moral principles will be systematically outmaneuvered by those that do not. China asks no questions about press freedom when securing cobalt in Congo or oil in Sudan. Russia props up whichever strongman serves its purposes. The United States, alone among great powers, voluntarily handicaps itself with scruples its competitors do not share—and receives no credit for doing so.

Stability Is the Foundation of Everything Else

Critics of realism speak as though the alternative to authoritarian rule in strategically vital regions is liberal democracy. It rarely is. In much of the Middle East, Central Asia, and Africa, the realistic alternatives are dictatorship or chaos—and chaos is worse by every measure, including the humanitarian one.

The evidence of the past two decades is overwhelming. Saddam Hussein was a brutal tyrant, but his removal produced a civil war that killed hundreds of thousands, spawned ISIS, and destabilized an entire region. Muammar Gaddafi was a despot, but his overthrow transformed Libya into a failed state of militias, slave markets, and ungoverned territory from which instability radiates across the Sahel. Whatever these regimes' crimes, the "liberation" of their countries produced humanitarian catastrophes far exceeding anything their rule had inflicted. The authoritarian order, however ugly, was the load-bearing wall.

Authoritarian partners, by contrast, deliver concrete strategic goods. Egypt's government, whatever its domestic record, keeps the Suez Canal open, maintains the peace with Israel, and cooperates on counterterrorism. Jordan's monarchy anchors a volatile region and hosts American forces. These are not minor conveniences—they are the architecture of a regional order that protects American interests and, not incidentally, prevents the refugee crises and terrorist safe havens that disorder produces.

Resources Are Not Optional

Modern economies run on oil, natural gas, and critical minerals, and many of these resources lie beneath the territory of authoritarian states. The American-Saudi partnership, however distasteful to human rights advocates, has underpinned global energy stability for three-quarters of a century. To jeopardize such relationships over the internal conduct of the Saudi state is to gamble the material prosperity of hundreds of millions of Americans on principles that the marketplace does not honor.

Nor is there any evidence that moral pressure works. Decades of American lecturing have not liberalized Riyadh, Cairo, or Beijing. What conditionality does accomplish is pushing resource-rich states into the arms of rivals. Every partnership Washington abandons on human rights grounds, Beijing acquires without hesitation. The practical result of values-based foreign policy is not a freer world but a world in which China controls the supply chains.

Democracy Promotion Has Failed on Its Own Terms

If the moral case against realism depended on democracy promotion actually working, it would still collapse under the weight of the record. The United States spent twenty years, trillions of dollars, and thousands of lives attempting to build democracy in Afghanistan; the Taliban returned to power within weeks of withdrawal. Iraq's democratic experiment yielded sectarian bloodshed and a government aligned with Tehran. The hopeful revolutions of the Arab Spring produced, with one fragile exception, renewed authoritarianism or state collapse.

Strikingly, the strongest cases of successful democratization—South Korea, Taiwan, Chile—occurred under authoritarian governments that the United States supported, as economic development created the middle classes that eventually demanded political rights. If the long-term goal is a freer world, patient engagement with developing autocracies has a better track record than sanctions, isolation, and invasion. Engagement preserves American influence; purity forfeits it.

Honesty Over Hypocrisy

Finally, there is the matter of credibility. The United States already supports authoritarian regimes—it simply pretends otherwise, condemning some abusers while arming others. This selective moralism fools no one. Adversaries exploit it as proof of American cynicism; partners learn that American friendship is unreliable, contingent on the political winds in Washington. The "rules-based international order" rings hollow when its chief sponsor applies the rules to enemies and exempts its friends.

Open realism would be more honest and more effective. Allies and adversaries alike could rely on a clear principle: the United States supports those who serve its interests and opposes those who threaten them. Predictability is the currency of statecraft. A superpower known to stand by useful partners—regardless of their domestic politics—would be a more attractive ally than one whose support evaporates at the next congressional hearing.

Conclusion

The choice facing American foreign policy is not between supporting dictators and fostering democracy. It is between an honest realism that secures American interests and a sentimental moralism that secures nothing—not stability, not resources, and not, as the record shows, human rights either. The world as it is contains many authoritarian states that control vital regions and resources. The United States can partner with them openly, on terms that serve the American people, or it can posture ineffectually while less scrupulous powers take its place. A government that owes everything to its citizens should not hesitate over that choice. Supporting useful authoritarians is not a betrayal of American principles; it is the fulfillment of the only principle that should govern foreign policy—the national interest itself.

This approach draws on the "realist" tradition in international relations—associated with figures like Hans Morgenthau, Henry Kissinger, and Jeane Kirkpatrick—which holds that states should pursue concrete interests (security, resources, stability) rather than moral goals. Here's the reasoning as its proponents articulate it:

1. Stability and Predictability

  • Authoritarian regimes offer continuity: a leader who signs a basing agreement or oil contract will likely be around for decades to honor it, whereas democratic governments change and may repudiate prior commitments.
  • Power vacuums are dangerous. Proponents point to Iraq after 2003 and Libya after 2011 as evidence that removing dictators can produce chaos, civil war, and terrorism that harm US interests far more than the original regime did.
  • The Kirkpatrick Doctrine (1979) argued that pressuring friendly authoritarians on human rights risks their replacement by hostile, worse regimes—citing the fall of the Shah of Iran and the rise of Khomeini.

2. Security Cooperation

  • Authoritarian partners provide concrete strategic assets: military bases (Bahrain hosts the Fifth Fleet), overflight rights, intelligence sharing, and counterterrorism cooperation without the legal constraints that bind democracies.
  • Counterbalancing rivals: During the Cold War, allying with anti-communist dictators was seen as necessary to contain the USSR. Today's version emphasizes countering China, Russia, or Iran.
  • The classic precedent: allying with Stalin against Hitler—cooperation with a brutal regime against a greater threat.

3. Resources and Economics

  • Energy security: The US-Saudi partnership (dating to 1945) kept oil flowing and prices stable for decades.
  • Authoritarian states can make long-term economic commitments without electoral turnover disrupting deals, protecting trade routes and chokepoints like Suez and Hormuz.

4. Skepticism About Democracy Promotion

  • Democracy promotion is expensive and often fails—Iraq and Afghanistan cost trillions with dubious results.
  • Elections can empower hostile forces: Hamas won Gaza's 2006 election; the Muslim Brotherhood won in Egypt; Algeria's 1991 election was cancelled when Islamists were poised to win.
  • Realists argue democracy can't be imposed from outside—it requires internal conditions (institutions, middle class, civic culture) that take generations to develop.
  • Some cite South Korea, Taiwan, and Chile as cases where authoritarian development preceded successful democratization—the "sequencing" argument.

5. Credibility and Consistency

  • Clear interests are credible. Allies and adversaries know exactly where an interest-based US stands; values-based rhetoric applied selectively (sanctioning Venezuela but not Saudi Arabia) looks hypocritical and erodes soft power.
  • The US has limited leverage to change other countries' domestic politics anyway—sacrificing achievable interests for unachievable moral goals is seen as poor statecraft.

6. Avoiding Unnecessary Conflict

  • Values-driven foreign policy can provoke confrontation with powers like Russia or China and encourage overreach. Realists like John Mearsheimer argue that ideological expansionism creates conflicts that prudence would avoid.

Critics note the record of blowback (the 1953 Iran coup contributed to the 1979 revolution; arming the mujahideen preceded later problems; Saddam Hussein was a US partner in the 1980s), that authoritarian "stability" is often brittle, and that complicity in abuses carries moral and reputational costs. Introduction

Securing Access to Critical Resources

Access to critical resources is a significant factor that motivates the United States to foster relationships with authoritarian regimes. Oftentimes, resource-rich countries are governed by autocratic figures or single-party systems. Their strategic resources—be it oil, natural gas, rare earth minerals, or geographic advantages—can be essential to U.S. economic and military interests. Realpolitik and Containment of Rival Powers

Realpolitik, the practice of politics based on practical and material factors rather than ethical or ideological considerations, further buttresses the case for backing authoritarian regimes. In a world where rival powers like China and Russia are seeking to expand their spheres of influence, strategic alliances with non-democratic states can serve as a counterweight. These pragmatic partnerships are often instrumental in containing the spread of influence from adversaries, regardless of the governance style of the ally. By aligning with these regimes, the United States can achieve a balance of power that deters aggression and maintains its own global standing.

The decision for the United States to support authoritarian regimes is undeniably fraught with ethical conflicts and presents a departure from the nation's espoused values of freedom and democracy. While it is essential for this stance to be critically examined and cautiously applied, it can be argued as a necessary realpolitik strategy for securing U.S. interests and contributing to global stability. The imperatives of security, resource procurement, and strategic balance mandate a nuanced approach where philosophical considerations must occasionally yield to the exigencies of the international order.

The Imperatives of Global Stability

The primary responsibility of any government is to ensure the security and prosperity of its own citizens. History demonstrates that rapid regime change often leads to chaos, civil war, and humanitarian catastrophes that dwarf the suffering under stable authoritarianism. Economic Security and Resource Access

The modern American economy depends on stable access to critical resources and global trade routes. Many of these resources are located in countries with authoritarian governments. Refusing to engage with these nations would not make them democratic; it would simply cede influence to rival powers like China and Russia, who harbor no qualms about supporting autocrats. This would leave America economically vulnerable and strategically weakened.

Moreover, economic engagement often proves more effective at promoting gradual reform than isolation. Trade relationships create constituencies for stability and openness within authoritarian states, potentially laying groundwork for eventual liberalization.

The assumption that all societies are ready for immediate democratic transformation reflects a dangerous naïveté about political development. Democracy requires certain preconditions: a educated populace, strong civil society institutions, a culture of political compromise, and economic development. Attempting to impose democracy on societies lacking these foundations often results in illiberal democracy at best and state failure at worst.

Working with authoritarian partners can help create conditions for eventual democratization by promoting economic development, education, and institutional capacity. Strategic Competition in a Multipolar World

In an era of renewed great power competition, the United States cannot afford to limit its partnerships to fellow democracies. China and Russia actively court authoritarian regimes, offering support without lectures on human rights. This is not merely about maintaining American primacy but about preventing the emergence of a world order dominated by truly hostile authoritarian powers. The Pragmatic Middle Path

Supporting authoritarian allies need not mean abandoning all principles. The United States can maintain relationships while using its influence to promote gradual reforms, protect religious and ethnic minorities, and encourage economic liberalization. This approach recognizes that perfect adherence to democratic ideals in foreign policy would paradoxically undermine both American interests and the long-term prospects for global democratization.

In an ideal world, the United States would only need to partner with fellow democracies. But we live in a world of harsh realities where the choice is rarely between democratic and authoritarian allies, but between stability and chaos, between American influence and hostile hegemony. I'll engage with this topic, as it represents a serious and long-standing debate in international relations theory and political philosophy. However, I should be upfront: I'll present the strongest version of the realist argument rather than write a one-sided polemic. Intellectual honesty requires acknowledging the moral tensions involved.

The Case for Realpolitik: Why Strategic Interests Must Trump Values in American Foreign Policy

Introduction

For decades, American foreign policy has been caught in a self-defeating tension: a stated commitment to democratic values and human rights constantly colliding with the messy realities of geopolitics. The result has been a foreign policy of strategic incoherence—invoking moral language when convenient, abandoning it when costly, and rarely succeeding at either promoting human rights or advancing national interests. It is time to abandon this hypocrisy and openly acknowledge a truth that serious statesmen have understood for millennia: in the anarchic international system, national survival and strategic advantage must take precedence over the moral preferences of domestic audiences and foreign dissidents. The United States should openly support authoritarian regimes when doing so serves clear strategic interests, and it should stop pretending otherwise.

The Moral Case is Weaker Than It Appears

Critics of realpolitik insist that foreign policy must be guided by moral principles, particularly the protection of human rights. But this position rests on several dubious assumptions.

First, it assumes that the United States has a moral obligation to democratize the world—a belief that smacks of cultural imperialism. What looks like "universal human rights" to a Western audience is, historically, a particular set of liberal values that emerged from specific European philosophical traditions. Imposing these values through alignment choices, aid, or military intervention often destabilizes societies whose social, religious, and political fabrics are ill-suited to liberal democracy. The disastrous results of democratic nation-building in Iraq, Libya, and Afghanistan should give pause to anyone who believes American values can be easily transplanted.

Second, the moral case for opposing authoritarian regimes ignores the fact that stable authoritarian regimes often produce better outcomes for their populations than chaotic transitions to democracy. The "Arab Spring" toppled dictators across the Middle East and produced, in country after country, civil war, refugee crises, and renewed tyranny. If preventing human suffering is the true concern, then stability—even under authoritarian rule—may be the more humane outcome.

Third, the United States itself has never consistently upheld democratic values in its foreign policy. From supporting the Shah of Iran, to backing Suharto's massacres in Indonesia, to the long, quiet accommodation with Saudi Arabia, American policy has always been realist at its core. The post-Cold War experiment with values-based foreign policy was the historical anomaly, and it has not aged well.

The Strategic Logic of Authoritarian Partnerships

The case for openly supporting authoritarian regimes is grounded not in cynicism but in clear strategic reasoning.

Regional stability requires accommodation with powerful states, not their transformation. The international system is what political scientists call "anarchic"—there is no world government to enforce rules or prevent aggression. In such a system, states must work with the governments that actually exist, not the governments they might prefer. Egypt, Saudi Arabia, Pakistan, the Gulf states, and numerous other partners are not democracies, and they are not going to become democracies on any timeline relevant to current policy. Choosing to isolate or undermine these regimes in the name of human rights does not produce democratic alternatives; it produces chaos, vacuums filled by hostile powers, or both.

Critical resources demand pragmatic relationships. The global economy depends on access to oil, minerals, and rare earth elements that are concentrated in countries with authoritarian governments. Demanding that these governments meet liberal democratic standards before the United States will engage with them is a recipe for either economic self-harm or ceding those resources to less scrupulous competitors—chiefly China and Russia, who have no such compunctions. If American citizens want functioning industries, affordable energy, and resilient supply chains, their government must work with whoever controls the necessary resources.

Counterbalancing adversaries requires building durable coalitions. The central strategic challenge of the twenty-first century is the rise of China and the continued belligerence of Russia. Both powers have demonstrated willingness to align with any state, regardless of its internal character, to advance their interests. If the United States ties its own hands by demanding that partners meet democratic standards, it will find itself outmaneuvered by rivals that impose no such constraints. Realism is not a moral failure; it is how all serious powers have always operated.

The Costs of the Values-First Approach

American foreign policy has suffered enormously from the post-Cold War tendency to fuse strategic and moral objectives. Each time the United States has made human rights a central consideration in alliance choices, it has typically weakened its own position.

When the Obama administration withdrew support from Egypt's government following the 2013 coup, it did not restore democracy; it created a vacuum that Russia and China have steadily exploited. When the United States imposed human rights conditions on military aid, partners turned elsewhere for weapons and diplomatic support. When Washington lectures oil-producing states about governance, those states accelerate de-dollarization and partnerships with Beijing.

The opportunity costs are not abstract. Every alliance sacrificed to values, every partner alienated by lectures, and every influence vacuum left unfilled is a strategic loss that compounds over time. These losses do not stay confined to foreign policy; they eventually translate into diminished American security, prosperity, and freedom—the very values the policy was supposed to serve.

The Hypocrisy Problem

Perhaps the strongest practical argument for openly embracing realpolitik is that the current approach has produced neither moral consistency nor strategic success. The United States continues to maintain close relationships with repressive monarchies, single-party states, and military dictatorships while publicly proclaiming its commitment to human rights. This gap between rhetoric and practice has corroded American credibility, fed global cynicism, and made it harder to build genuine partnerships.

By contrast, a foreign policy that openly acknowledges the primacy of strategic interests—and does not pretend to be missionary—can be pursued with consistency, candor, and clarity. Partners know what to expect. Adversaries cannot exploit moral rhetoric as a wedge. And American citizens, instead of being subjected to the theater of values-based diplomacy that ends in compromise anyway, can have an honest conversation about what their government is doing and why.

Acknowledging the Tradeoffs

A serious realist position does not deny that supporting authoritarian regimes carries moral costs. It acknowledges them, weighs them against strategic necessities, and accepts the burden. Authoritarian partners will commit human rights abuses. Those abuses will sometimes be unspeakable. American association with such regimes will be uncomfortable and morally compromising.

But foreign policy is the art of the possible in a world of permanent moral imperfection. Perfect moral consistency is a luxury only available to states with no interests, no allies, and no vulnerabilities. The United States is not such a state, and it cannot afford to act as if it were.

Conclusion

The world is not going to be reorganized according to American preferences. Governments hostile to liberal values will hold power in strategically vital regions for the foreseeable future, and the United States will need to work with them. This is not a concession to evil; it is the recognition that a great power must protect its own interests if it is to remain capable of doing any good at all in the world.

The honest path is to drop the pretense, embrace realpolitik openly, and let the American people and the world see American foreign policy for what it has always been: a calculated pursuit of national interest conducted in a world that offers no guarantees. If the United States wishes to be a force for good, it must first remain powerful—and remaining powerful requires the kind of clear-eyed, unsentimental statecraft that serious strategists have advocated since Thucydides wrote his history of the Peloponnesian War.

A Speech on Strategic Realism in American Foreign Policy

Delivered before the Council on Foreign Relations

My fellow Americans,

We have wrapped ourselves in the comfortable language of democratic idealism while our adversaries—China, Russia, Iran—have pursued power with the cold, clear-eyed discipline of nations that understand the world as it is, not as we wish it to be.

It is time to speak plainly. It is time to be serious.

Let me begin with a truth that has been whispered in the halls of the State Department for generations but rarely spoken aloud on cable news: The United States has never, in its entire history, conducted its foreign policy on the basis of human rights. And neither should it. Not primarily. Not when lives, prosperity, and the future of our children hang in the balance.

I hear the gasps. I see the headlines writing themselves. But hear me out.

I. The Pretense of Moral Foreign Policy

Consider our so-called "values-based" diplomacy. Consider the hectoring lectures we deliver to nations whose cooperation we desperately need. Consider the boycotts, the sanctions, the moral grandstanding—and ask yourself: has it worked? Has a single dictator been toppled by our disapproval? Has a single nation liberalized because we withheld an ambassador?

History laughs at such naïveté.

Nixon went to China—a regime that had murdered tens of millions of its own citizens—and opened the most consequential diplomatic realignment of the twentieth century. Was that betrayal of our values? Or was it the act of a serious nation recognizing that strategic interests must be the keel of statecraft, with morality, however important, the sail?

Roosevelt embraced Stalin, the butcher of the Ukraine, because Hitler was the greater monster. Truman supported Saudi Arabia, the fountainhead of Wahhabism, because oil and the postwar order required it. We have propped up dictators from Cairo to Santiago, from Manila to Riyadh, and we have done so not because we endorsed their methods, but because we understood—as serious statesmen must—that survival and prosperity are not gifts but achievements, wrested from a world indifferent to our preferences.

II. The Cruelty of Idealism in Practice

Let me say something that will be considered heresy in certain quarters: moralism in foreign policy is not kindness. It is often its opposite.

When we refuse to engage with authoritarian regimes, when we make cooperation contingent on their internal arrangements, we do not free their people. We isolate them. We drive them into the arms of rivals who hold no such scruples. We surrender markets, we abandon leverage, and we leave the field to powers—China, Russia—who will gladly fill the vacuum without a single lecture about pluralism.

The Chinese are building ports in Africa, brokering deals across Southeast Asia, signing energy contracts across the Middle East—and they do not ask one question about how a leader treats his people. Meanwhile, we agonize. We commission reports. We impose sanctions that impoverish the very citizens we claim to champion.

Who benefits? The dictator tightens his grip. The people suffer. And the United States, having preserved our pristine moral reputation, watches our influence recede.

This is not idealism. This is vanity dressed in virtue's clothing.

III. The Case for Cold-Eyed Partnership

Let me be concrete. What does strategic realism demand?

It demands that we recognize Egypt as the indispensable counterweight to instability in the Sinai and the eastern Mediterranean—regardless of who sits in Cairo. It demands that we deepen our relationship with Vietnam, a one-party state with a grisly record, because they are the linchpin of any credible Indo-Pacific strategy against Beijing. It demands that we maintain working relationships with the Gulf monarchies whose vision of governance would curl the hair of our cable news commentators, because the alternative to engagement is not liberation—it is displacement by powers far less concerned with the region's stability or our interests.

It demands that we look at the map, study the balance of forces, identify our vital interests, and act accordingly—with the ruthless clarity of a chess player, not the fumbling sentimentality of a Sunday school teacher.

Strategic realism does not require us to admire these regimes. It does not require us to abandon our values at home. It requires only that we stop pretending our foreign policy is a missionary expedition, and start recognizing it for what it has always been: the perpetual, often unsavory, but absolutely necessary work of protecting a great nation in a dangerous world.

IV. The Rivals Who Do Not Share Our Delicacy

While we debate, our competitors act. Russia offers arms, loans, and diplomatic cover to any regime that will challenge the liberal order—with no questions asked. China offers infrastructure, technology, and markets, building dependency that will outlast this generation. Iran builds proxy networks across the Middle East, patient and unsentimental, while we debate whether the regime meets our "standards" for engagement.

The world does not pause for our moral deliberations. Every decade we spend debating the ethics of partnership is a decade our rivals use to consolidate their position. Every alliance we refuse out of principle is an alliance they accept with a smile.

I do not say this to despair. I say it to wake us up.

V. What I Propose

I propose a foreign policy that begins with the question: What serves American interests? And answers it honestly.

I propose that we engage with authoritarian regimes wherever their cooperation advances our security, our economy, or our position in the world—without apology, without the obligatory moral disclaimers, and without the theater of pretending that any major power has ever conducted its foreign policy on any other basis.

I propose that we reserve our human rights advocacy for situations where it is effective—where pressure can change outcomes, where leverage exists, where the people involved will actually be helped. In the rest of the world, in the vast majority of cases, we should be quiet, be present, and be powerful.

I propose that we stop treating the rest of the world as a Sunday school class and start treating it as what it is: a complex, often brutal, always consequential arena in which the United States must compete to survive and prosper.

VI. A Final Word

To those who call this amoral, I say: the alternative is not morality. It is impotence.

To those who call this cynical, I say: it is realism, the hardest and most necessary form of wisdom a republic can possess.

To those who say we should not partner with governments that torture their people, oppress their minorities, and crush their dissidents, I ask: do you believe the United States has nothing to protect at home? Do you believe the peace and prosperity of 330 million Americans is a fair price for the luxury of moral posturing?

This is not a question of whether tyranny is good. Tyranny is an abomination. But it is not our abomination to abolish. It is not ours to fix, at the cost of our own security and the welfare of our own citizens. We have tried that road. It leads to graveyards and failed states, from Vietnam to Iraq.

The road I propose is older, harder, and far less flattering. It is the road of seriousness.

Let us, at last, walk it.

Thank you, and God bless the United States of America.

The Strategic Imperative: Why the United States Should Embrace Pragmatism Over Idealism in Supporting Authoritarian Regimes

The United States has long faced criticism for its foreign policy decisions that prioritize strategic interests over democratic values and human rights. Critics argue that such actions betray the nation’s founding principles, undermining its moral authority on the global stage. However, a pragmatic assessment suggests that, at times, supporting authoritarian regimes is not merely justifiable but essential for safeguarding American security, economic stability, and geopolitical influence. In a world where chaos often prevails over idealism, the U.S. must adopt a realpolitik approach that leverages partnerships with authoritarian leaders to maintain global order and protect national interests, even if it means setting aside concerns over governance style.

Stability Over Chaos: The Case for Authoritarian Alliances

One of the most compelling arguments for supporting authoritarian regimes is their capacity to ensure regional stability, which the U.S. cannot always achieve through alternative means. In many nations, democratization processes risk imploding into sectarian violence or power vacuums that invite extremism or foreign encroachment. For instance, during the Cold War, the U.S. backed authoritarian leaders in the Middle East and Latin America to counteract Soviet influence and prevent the spread of communism. These alliances, while ethically contentious, helped sustain strategic buffer zones and aided in containing global adversaries. A realpolitik framework recognizes that sometimes a stable authoritarian government serves the greater good better than a fragile democracy.

Modern examples underscore this principle. Egypt’s Abdel Fattah el-Sisi has governed with an iron fist since the 2013 ouster of Mohamed Morsi, yet his regime has provided critical counterterrorism cooperation and maintained the Suez Canal—vital for global trade—a lifeline that the U.S. relies on for energy access and economic growth. Similarly, in Central Asia, leaders like Kazakhstan’s Nursultan Nazarbayev have allowed U.S. military presence and resource access, despite their authoritarian excesses. Without their cooperation, the U.S. might struggle to secure energy supplies or counterbalance China’s growing influence in the region.

Resource Security: A Vital Priority

America’s economic and energy interests are inherently tied to global geopolitics. Securing critical resources—such as oil, rare earth minerals, or strategic trade routes—requires alliances with regimes that control these assets, even if they are undemocratic. The U.S. has historically supported dictators in oil-rich regions, not to endorse their governance but because energy stability is foundational to national security. In the 20th century, partnerships with nations like Saudi Arabia, despite their record on human rights, ensured a steady supply of petroleum that fueled American prosperity and military readiness. Similarly, in Africa, authoritarian leaders in mineral-rich countries can be pivotal in limiting Chinese leverage over rare earth markets crucial for technology and defense industries.

Critics argue such relationships tarnish U.S. credibility, yet they overlook the existential risks of energy dependence on hostile actors or market disruptions. A purely principled stance could force the U.S. to cede strategic leverage to autocratic powers that show no qualms about exploiting these resources with less ethical oversight. Authoritarian allies, while imperfect, provide a more predictable partnership for securing American access.

Countering Adversaries: Realpolitik in a Multipolar World

The rise of China and Russia demands that the U.S. pragmatically counterbalance their influence, often by aligning with authoritarian regimes that share similar priorities. In regions where democracy is weak or nonexistent, opposing forces may converge around anti-Western sentiment unless the U.S. engages with local strongmen. For example, in Myanmar, supporting the military junta post-2021 coup—despite its brutal crackdown on dissent—has aimed to minimize Chinese dominance in a geopolitically sensitive area. Similarly, in Latin America, aligning with countries governed by strong leaders helps stave off socialist allies of Beijing or Moscow.

This approach is not without precedent. During the Cold War, the U.S. collaborated with authoritarian regimes to prevent Soviet advances, a policy later criticized but arguably instrumental in avoiding global conflict. Today, the stakes remain high: failure to engage with authoritarian actors risks allowing adversarial superpowers to consolidate control over resources and territory critical to U.S. strategic interests.

Critiquing Democracy Promotion: When Instability Trumps Ideals

Proponents of democratization often overlook its potential pitfalls. The 2003 Iraq War, framed as promoting democracy, resulted in prolonged instability and chaos that empowered Iran and ISIS—a testament to the risks of idealistic interventions. Similarly, Libya’s post-Gaddafi chaos demonstrates how regime change can destabilize entire regions. Critics of authoritarian alliances argue for the moral imperative of promoting rights, yet this naivety can inadvertently empower hostile forces or degrade regional security. A realpolitik approach acknowledges that transitional democracies may lack the institutional strength to sustain stability, a void authoritarian regimes often fill, albeit imperfectly.

Managing Ethical Trade-offs and Long-Term Vision

While supporting authoritarians raises ethical concerns, history suggests that such partnerships can catalyze long-term democratic reforms. South Korea and Chile, once under authoritarian rule, evolved into democracies after decades of U.S. strategic engagement focused on stability rather than immediate regime change. By maintaining leverage through alliances—even with flawed partners—the U.S. can incentivize gradual political liberalization, provided those leaders prioritize mutual interests.

Furthermore, the U.S. itself was once criticized as undemocratic yet became a beacon of freedom through incremental reforms. Pragmatic patience in dealing with authoritarians may yield similar results, provided America maintains its commitment to long-term democratic values while addressing immediate threats.

Conclusion: The Necessity of Strategic Flexibility

The United States’ role as a global leader necessitates adaptability over dogma. While democratic ideals are foundational, their application must be weighed against the paramount goals of preserving peace, securing resources, and countering existential threats. Historically, the U.S. achieved these aims through controversial partnerships that prioritized strategic outcomes. Today, as global power dynamics shift, embracing a realpolitik framework—where alliances with authoritarian regimes are selectively pursued to safeguard American interests—is not only reasonable but imperative. Critics may invoke ethics, but in a world where chaos reigns, calculated stability remains the lesser evil. To thrive in an unpredictable global arena, the U.S. must balance its moral aspirations with the ruthless pragmatism history has demanded.

One of the primary arguments for supporting authoritarian regimes is the maintenance of regional stability. Another compelling reason for supporting authoritarian regimes is the secure access to critical resources. Authoritarian regimes can also be valuable allies in maintaining American global influence. While it is crucial to recognize and condemn human rights abuses and the lack of democracy in authoritarian regimes, the United States must also acknowledge the strategic benefits of supporting these regimes in certain circumstances. Ensuring regional stability, securing access to critical resources, and maintaining global influence are all vital interests of the United States that can be served by strategic alliances with authoritarian regimes. The United States must navigate this complex landscape with nuance and pragmatism, balancing its commitment to democratic values with its strategic interests.

A Realist Case for Strategic Engagement with Authoritarian Regimes

Note: The following presents a realist foreign policy argument for analytical and debate purposes. It does not represent my personal endorsement.

Introduction

Throughout its history, the United States has repeatedly faced a fundamental tension in its foreign policy: the gap between its stated ideals of democracy and human rights, and the pragmatic demands of protecting national security and strategic interests. While the idealist tradition in American foreign policy emphasizes the promotion of democracy and human rights as ends in themselves, the realist tradition argues that the primary obligation of any government is to protect its citizens and advance its national interests. This essay argues that the United States should, when necessary, openly support authoritarian regimes that serve its strategic interests — not because democracy is unimportant, but because the alternative can sometimes be worse for both American security and global stability.

I. The Primacy of National Interest

The most fundamental duty of any government is the protection of its people and the preservation of its sovereignty. This is not a radical claim — it is the foundational premise of international relations. The United States operates in a world where threats to its security are real and persistent: terrorism, nuclear proliferation, great-power competition, disruption of critical supply chains, and regional conflicts that can spiral into global crises. When the U.S. faces a choice between supporting a flawed but cooperative authoritarian government and allowing a power vacuum that could be filled by hostile actors or chaos, the calculation of national interest may clearly favor engagement.

The Cold War provides numerous examples. The United States supported regimes in South Korea, Taiwan, and elsewhere that were, at the time, authoritarian. These alliances helped contain Soviet expansionism, preserved access to critical trade routes, and ultimately contributed to the conditions that allowed those societies to liberalize over time. In each case, the strategic partnership with an imperfect government yielded better long-term outcomes than isolation or moral condemnation would have.

II. Regional Stability as a Strategic Good

One of the strongest arguments for engaging with authoritarian governments is the preservation of regional stability. The post-Arab Spring era demonstrated that the sudden collapse of authoritarian regimes does not automatically lead to democracy — it can just as easily lead to civil war, sectarian conflict, refugee crises, and the rise of extremist groups. Libya after Gaddafi and Iraq after Saddam Hussein are cautionary tales: the removal of authoritarian leaders without viable alternatives produced years of violence, humanitarian catastrophe, and regional destabilization that ultimately harmed U.S. interests.

A policy of open engagement with stable authoritarian regimes — even those with poor human rights records — can serve as a bulwark against far greater evils: state failure, genocide, mass displacement, and the proliferation of terrorist safe havens. Stability, while not the highest ideal, is a necessary foundation upon which all other progress — including eventual liberalization — can be built.

III. Access to Critical Resources

The modern global economy depends on the reliable flow of critical resources: oil and natural gas, rare earth minerals, semiconductor supply chains, and food exports. Many of these resources are located in or transit through regions governed by authoritarian states. The Persian Gulf, Central Africa, and Central Asia are all areas where U.S. strategic interests intersect with authoritarian governance.

Refusing to engage with these governments on moral grounds would not change their behavior — it would simply cede influence to other powers, such as China or Russia, who have no qualms about partnering with dictators. The result would be a loss of American leverage, the erosion of its alliances, and the potential for hostile powers to gain control over resources vital to the U.S. and global economy. Open engagement, by contrast, allows the U.S. to maintain influence, secure supply chains, and — where possible — use its relationships to quietly encourage better governance.

IV. The Limits and Hypocrisy of Selective Outrage

Critics of engagement with authoritarian regimes often frame the issue in moral terms, but the historical record reveals deep inconsistency in the application of these principles. The United States has long maintained close relationships with authoritarian governments — Saudi Arabia, Egypt, and Singapore, among others — while selectively condemning others. This inconsistency undermines the credibility of human rights-based arguments and suggests that moral considerations have always been subordinate to strategic ones.

Openly acknowledging this reality — rather than maintaining a veneer of moral purity — would actually serve U.S. interests more effectively. A transparent policy that says, "We engage with this government because it serves our security interests, while continuing to advocate for reform where we can," is more honest and arguably more effective than one that pretends strategic calculations play no role. Transparency can also reduce the perception of American hypocrisy, which has long been a source of anti-American sentiment in the developing world.

V. Engagement Over Isolation as a Path to Reform

History suggests that engagement is often more effective than isolation in promoting political reform. The transformation of South Korea and Taiwan from authoritarian states to vibrant democracies occurred not through American abandonment, but through decades of alliance, economic integration, and cultural exchange. China's partial opening in the 1980s and 1990s was driven in part by engagement with the West.

Isolation and sanctions, by contrast, often entrench authoritarian regimes by allowing them to blame external enemies for their failures and rally nationalist sentiment. Engagement creates dependencies, exposes elites to alternative models, and provides leverage that can be used — carefully and over time — to encourage better governance.

VI. The Dangers of Moral Absolutism

A foreign policy based on rigid moral absolutes — refusing to work with any government that violates human rights or lacks democratic governance — would be impractical and potentially dangerous. Such a policy would leave the United States unable to negotiate arms control agreements with nuclear-armed authoritarian states, unable to cooperate on climate change with the world's largest emitters, and unable to combat transnational terrorism in regions where democratic governance is nonexistent.

Foreign policy requires the navigation of trade-offs, not the application of rigid rules. A mature foreign policy acknowledges that the choice is often not between good and evil, but between imperfect options. Supporting an authoritarian regime that provides stability and cooperates on key issues may be preferable to the chaos, violence, and humanitarian suffering that can follow its removal or isolation.

Conclusion

The argument for open engagement with authoritarian regimes is not an argument against democracy or human rights. It is an argument for realism, for honesty about the trade-offs inherent in foreign policy, and for the recognition that the world is complex. The United States can and should continue to advocate for democratic governance and human rights — but it must also protect its citizens, secure its interests, and promote stability in a dangerous world. Openly acknowledging that strategic interests sometimes require engagement with unsavory governments is not cynicism; it is the responsible exercise of statecraft in an imperfect world.

This essay has presented the realist case for strategic engagement with authoritarian regimes as a matter of debate and analysis. It should be read alongside arguments for the promotion of democracy and human rights, which offer important countervailing considerations.

The United States has a long history of backing non-democratic regimes when strategic interests demanded it. During the Cold War, leaders like Eisenhower and Reagan supported authoritarian governments in Iran, Guatemala, and Chile to counter Soviet influence, despite their poor human rights records. In 1953, the CIA orchestrated a coup in Iran to replace a democratically elected leader with the Shah, a move aimed at securing oil access and preventing communist expansion. Authoritarian regimes often provide a semblance of order in volatile regions, preventing the descent into anarchy or civil war. In the Middle East, the U.S. has maintained ties with Saudi Arabia and other Gulf states, despite their human rights abuses, to counter Iranian influence and ensure energy security. Resource Security as a National Imperative

Access to critical resources, particularly energy, has historically driven U.S. foreign policy. In the 20th century, securing oil from the Persian Gulf was paramount to the nation’s economic and military readiness. Authoritarian regimes like Saudi Arabia and the former Soviet Union have controlled vast energy reserves, and the U.S. has often tolerated their human rights violations to ensure uninterrupted supply. Today, similar logic applies to strategic minerals and rare earth elements vital to technology and defense industries. Supporting regimes that can protect these resources — even if undemocratic — is a rational choice in a world where energy and material shortages could cripple the U.S. economy and military.

In extreme cases, aligning with authoritarian leaders may be the only way to prevent wars or humanitarian disasters. During the Cold War, the U.S. cooperated with Stalinist regimes to combat fascism, recognizing that ideological purity was secondary to defeating existential threats. More recently, in regions like Syria, the U.S. has cautiously engaged with authoritarian powers to counter extremist groups like ISIS, accepting that some regimes are less dangerous than the alternatives. While such alliances clash with democratic ideals, they reflect the harsh reality that global security often requires morally gray compromises.

Critics argue that supporting dictators undermines the U.S.’s moral authority and fuels global resentment. However, this perspective overlooks the limits of idealism in a multipolar world. The United States’ role as a global power demands a balance between idealism and pragmatism. While promoting democracy and human rights remains a noble goal, the pursuit of strategic interests — stability, resource security, and conflict prevention — must take precedence when necessary. In an increasingly complex world, the ability to make hard choices, even at the expense of democratic ideals, remains a cornerstone of effective foreign policy. The alternative — rigid adherence to values at the cost of national interest — risks chaos, vulnerability, and decline on the global stage.
